title: S&P cuts Salesforce to ’A’ on rising acquisition debt and buybacks
detail:
S&P cuts Salesforce to ’A’ on rising acquisition debt and buybacks
Luke Juricic
Wed, November 4, 2026 at 1:44 PM MST 2 min read
SPGI
CRM
BRZE
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investing.com -- S&P Global Ratings downgraded Salesforce Inc (NYSE:CRM) to 'A' from 'A+', pointing to an increasingly aggressive capital allocation strategy characterized by debt-funded shareholder returns and large-scale acquisitions. The ratings agency highlighted that recent dealmaking, alongside a $25 billion debt-financed share repurchase program, has pushed pro forma net debt-to-EBITDA above its previous 2x downgrade threshold.

The rating action reflects mounting risks that leverage could climb further as the enterprise software maker pursues an ambitious long-term expansion blueprint. S&P expects management will prioritize growth investments and buybacks over balance-sheet cash accumulation to reach its goal of expanding revenue from approximately $44 billion today to more than $63 billion by 2030.

That expansion push has already catalyzed significant deal activity, including pending or completed takeovers of Informatica for $9.5 billion, Braze for $5.7 billion, and Fin for $3.6 billion. S&P noted that Salesforce's organic revenue momentum has moderated, leaving the company increasingly reliant on programmatic M&A to generate 3 to 4 percentage points of its projected 11% fiscal 2027 top-line growth.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

Near-term execution across core subscription operations remains solid, anchored by a 14% year-over-year lift in remaining performance obligations during the second quarter. While growth across the company's marketing and commerce offerings has softened recently, S&P indicated the Braze transaction could help reverse that trend and reinforce cross-selling momentum.

Longer term, Salesforce is directing resources toward monetizing its Data360 and Agentforce frameworks, which generated $3.9 billion in annual recurring revenue in the second quarter. Strong adoption of agentic AI offerings could lift customer spending by 1.5x to 2.0x and mitigate seat attrition risks, though the agency cautioned that material top-line contributions are unlikely over the next two fiscal years.

S&P assigned a stable outlook to the revised rating, projecting that strong free operating cash flow will allow Salesforce to sustain net leverage below 2.5x while defending its enterprise footprint. The agency warned, however, that further debt-funded buybacks, larger transactions pushing leverage beyond 2.5x, or disruptive AI competition could trigger additional downward rating pressure.

title: Salesforce Stock Has Only Done This Twice Before. Here's What History Suggests Happens Next.
detail:
Salesforce Stock Has Only Done This Twice Before. Here's What History Suggests Happens Next.
Jake Lerch, The Motley Fool
Wed, November 4, 2026 at 11:50 AM MST 5 min read
CRM
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

What's your first thought when you see "half off" at the bakery? Are you eager to snap up a quick deal, or do you assume the bread's gone stale? A similar question emerges in the stock market.

Take Salesforce (NYSE: CRM), for example. The company's stock has endured a rough patch over the last two years. At its June 2026 low, the stock had dropped more than 59% from its all-time high.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

But to decide whether Salesforce is a ready-made bargain or a week-old baguette, we need to examine the details.

Image source: Getty Images.
Salesforce's 50% stock declines are rare

Salesforce has been a public company since 2004. In its more than 22 years as a public company, its stock has dropped 50% or more from its all-time high on only three occasions:

CRM data by YCharts

Oct. 7, 2008: Salesforce stock fell sharply, along with the broader market, as the financial crisis shook Wall Street. Salesforce stock ultimately declined by 70% before bottoming in November 2008.

Sept. 1, 2022: Salesforce stock melted slowly throughout late 2021 and nearly all of 2022 during the latest bear market. After crossing the 50% threshold in September 2022, the stock bottomed in December 2022, down 59% from its all-time high, before recovering and setting new all-time highs in 2024.

Feb. 23, 2026: Salesforce stock fell below the 50% mark in February 2026 as market participants fretted over whether software-as-a-service (SaaS) business models would withstand rapid innovations in the artificial intelligence (AI) sector.

These drops aren't garden-variety pullbacks; they are rare structural resets. And in the latest case, a recovery may already be underway.

Past recoveries rewarded patience, not perfect timing

So, let's see what happened in the past. In each case, we'll assume an investor bought the day after the 50% level was crossed. In the 2008 case, shares gained 63% in the year after the breach. In 2022, Salesforce stock rose 44% in the following 12 months. However, there's one very important caveat: Things got worse before they got better. In 2008, shares dropped another 39% before the bottom was truly in. In 2022, shares fell another 16%.

In other words, while a 50% drop is massive for Salesforce stock, investors shouldn't think of it as a line in the sand. The stock can -- and has -- fallen even further before. Past rebounds show resilience, but today's recovery requires a clear-eyed look at the current business.

title: Salesforce (CRM) Moves to Strong Buy: Rationale Behind the Upgrade

Salesforce (CRM) Moves to Strong Buy: Rationale Behind the Upgrade
Zacks Equity Research

CRM
Trade CRM on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investors might want to bet on Salesforce (CRM), as it has been recently upgraded to a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy). This upgrade primarily reflects an upward trend in earnings estimates, which is one of the most powerful forces impacting stock prices.

The sole determinant of the Zacks rating is a company's changing earnings picture. The Zacks Consensus Estimate -- the consensus of EPS estimates from the sell-side analysts covering the stock -- for the current and following years is tracked by the system.

Since a changing earnings picture is a powerful factor influencing near-term stock price movements, the Zacks rating system is very useful for individual investors. They may find it difficult to make decisions based on rating upgrades by Wall Street analysts, as these are mostly driven by subjective factors that are hard to see and measure in real time.

As such, the Zacks rating upgrade for Salesforce is essentially a positive comment on its earnings outlook that could have a favorable impact on its stock price.

Most Powerful Force Impacting Stock Prices

The change in a company's future earnings potential, as reflected in earnings estimate revisions, and the near-term price movement of its stock are proven to be strongly correlated. The influence of institutional investors has a partial contribution to this relationship, as these big professionals use earnings and earnings estimates to calculate the fair value of a company's shares. An increase or decrease in earnings estimates in their valuation models simply results in higher or lower fair value for a stock, and institutional investors typically buy or sell it. Their bulk investment action then leads to price movement for the stock.

Fundamentally speaking, rising earnings estimates and the consequent rating upgrade for Salesforce imply an improvement in the company's underlying business. Investors should show their appreciation for this improving business trend by pushing the stock higher.

Harnessing the Power of Earnings Estimate Revisions

Empirical research shows a strong correlation between trends in earnings estimate revisions and near-term stock movements, so it could be truly rewarding if such revisions are tracked for making an investment decision. Here is where the tried-and-tested Zacks Rank stock-rating system plays an important role, as it effectively harnesses the power of earnings estimate revisions.

The Zacks Rank stock-rating system, which uses four factors related to earnings estimates to classify stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), has an impressive externally-audited track record, with Zacks Rank #1 stocks generating an average annual return of +25% since 1988. Microsoft (MSFT) stock returned 27.2% between May 5 and November 3, 2026, compared with a 4.8% return for the S&P 500. During its October 28 call, management said customer demand still exceeds the capacity it has. The company also said that some third-party capacity it had counted on moved into the second half of the fiscal year. Below are the dates most likely to move Microsoft stock over the next six months, and the three that matter most.

Azure Growth In Microsoft's Next Report

Microsoft is expected to report its fiscal Q2 2027 results in January 2027. For that quarter, management guided Azure revenue growth of 49% to 50% in constant currency, following 48% growth in fiscal Q1 2027.

Azure operates inside Microsoft Cloud. That broader group brought in $63.9 billion in fiscal Q1 2027, about two-thirds of the company's revenue. Management said it is counting on more efficiency gains across its CPU and GPU fleet to reach the guide, because some third-party GPU contracts slipped into the second half of fiscal 2027. Measured against that guide, Azure growth in constant currency is the number to watch in the January 2027 report.

Microsoft's Rising Capital Spending

Management expects capital spending of over $50 billion in fiscal Q2 2027. The company currently expects spending to speed up in the second half of fiscal 2027, mainly on CPUs, GPUs, higher memory and storage costs and the delayed third-party capacity.

That is a large outlay even for Microsoft. Management put calendar 2026 spending at about $170 billion, close to half of the $346 billion of revenue the company took in over the last twelve months. Management expects Microsoft to stay free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027, and said it will tap other sources of funding when it finds them attractive. Capital spending and free cash flow are the figures to watch in the January 2027 report.

Xbox Holiday Game Sales

Microsoft entered the holiday season with one of its strongest first- and third-party game lineups in years, management said on October 28. That roster includes Grand Theft Auto VI, which the company said was coming to Xbox the following month.

title: Is There A Risk Hiding In Salesforce Stock's Record Quarter?

Is There A Risk Hiding In Salesforce Stock's Record Quarter?

Image from Pexels

For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Salesforce (CRM) called its fiscal Q2 2027 a record second quarter. When that period ended on July 31, 2026, the company owed $41.7 billion in total debt, a sum close to the $43.9 billion of revenue it brought in over the past twelve months. Any cash used to pay down that debt is cash that cannot go to shareholders. So how much more does Salesforce owe than it did a year ago?

Salesforce Owes Far More Than A Year Ago

Salesforce owed $11.2 billion at the end of July 2025, meaning it accumulated most of its July 2026 debt load in a single year. That pace breaks from the company's past. Over the five years leading up to July 2025, debt balances at the end of each July stayed between $11.2 billion and $15.5 billion.

Two other items changed over those same twelve months. Salesforce spent $35.1 billion buying back its own shares, up from $6.22 billion the year before, and management said on the August 26, 2026, call that its $25 billion accelerated share repurchase continues. At the same time, its cash and short-term investments fell to $11.4 billion, dropping from $15.4 billion a year earlier.

How Long Would Salesforce Need To Repay Its Debt?

Salesforce would need about two years of free cash flow to clear its debt after cash. The company owed $30.3 billion more than it held in cash and short-term investments, compared with $15.2 billion of free cash flow generated over the past twelve months.

Salesforce also has fewer shares to absorb that debt. Diluted shares fell to 821 million, down from 962 million a year earlier, and management expects to repurchase at least 14% of shares outstanding through the accelerated program, which by the August call had been buying shares at an average price of $176. Each remaining share now holds a larger slice of both the profit and the debt.

Measured against the company's market value, the debt load is modest, though above the market's. Salesforce's debt equals 22.9% of its market value, compared with 19.2% for the S&P 500.

What Are Investors Paying For Salesforce Today?

Investors are paying less for each dollar of cash Salesforce brings in than they do across the broader market. The stock trades at 11.6 times its cash from operations, trailing the 15.1 multiple for the S&P 500. Over the past year, through November 3, 2026, the shares lost 13.9%, while the S&P 500 returned 11.9%. The price likely assumes some of this risk already.

The business gives a holder reasons for calm. Free cash flow over the past twelve months reached $15.2 billion, up from $12.5 billion a year earlier, and management said on the August call that customer attrition was near its lowest level ever. Against that, news reports said on October 20, 2026, that Salesforce has agreed to buy Braze in a $5.66 billion deal, adding a further commitment on top of the buyback.

Docusign vs. Okta: Which Tech Stock Is a Better Buy for 2027?

As digital workflows become standard, many investors are choosing between the leader in electronic signatures and the titan of identity security. Here is how Docusign (NASDAQ:DOCU) and Okta (NASDAQ:OKTA) compare today.

Docusign focuses on automating agreement workflows through its Intelligent Agreement Management platform. Okta operates as a leader in identity security, ensuring only authorized users access corporate systems. While both provide critical cloud services, their growth profiles and market valuations offer distinct paths for investors looking ahead to 2027.

The case for Docusign

Docusign provides cloud-based software that simplifies the way organizations prepare, sign, and manage agreements. According to its latest annual report, filed for the period ending in early 2026, its Intelligent Agreement Management platform serves over 1.8 million customers globally. The company relies on deep integrations with partners like Salesforce (NYSE:CRM), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), and SAP (NYSE:SAP) to drive its product adoption.

In fiscal 2026, revenue reached nearly $3.2 billion, representing growth of approximately 8.2% over the prior year. This steady expansion is supported by a broad international presence in over 180 countries. The company reported net income of roughly $309.1 million during this period, showing continued profitability even as it invests in new artificial intelligence agreement features to remain competitive.

Docusign maintains a healthy balance sheet with a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.1, which measures total debt against shareholder equity. As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the current ratio is 0.7, which compares a company's short-term assets to its short-term liabilities. Free cash flow, which is cash from operations minus capital expenditures, reached approximately $1.1 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 53.4% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, as SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Okta

Okta provides identity and access management solutions to more than 20,000 customers globally, including large Fortune 50 enterprises and government agencies. Its latest annual report highlights a land-and-expand sales model used to increase its footprint among tech stocks. It manages an extensive integration network featuring over 7,000 connections with various cloud and mobile applications.

In fiscal 2026, revenue reached nearly $2.9 billion, representing approximately 11.8% growth over the previous year. This double-digit revenue increase remains higher than that of its e-signature peer, reflecting strong demand for cloud-based identity security. The company reported net income of roughly $235 million, a significant improvement from the fiscal year ended in 2024, when it reported a net loss.
